paragraphs.heading: What a turbidite is
paragraphs.text: A turbidite is the deposit left by a turbidity current. Turbidity currents are responsible for spreading vast amounts of clastic sediment into the deep ocean. Turbidites are carried and laid down by density flow, not by tractional or frictional flow.

paragraphs.heading: How a river moves a grain
paragraphs.text: In an ordinary river or stream bed, particles of rock are carried by the frictional drag of the water on each particle. This is called tractional flow. The water has to travel at a certain velocity to suspend the particle and push it along. The larger or denser the particle is compared with the fluid, the higher the velocity needed to suspend and transport it.

paragraphs.heading: How a density flow does it
paragraphs.text: Density-based flow happens when sediment liquefies during transport and changes the density of the fluid. This usually comes about in highly turbulent liquid carrying a suspended load of fine particles, which forms a slurry. Water plus sediment is denser than water alone, and so it is closer to the density of the rock. With that lower contrast, larger rock fragments can be moved at water velocities too low to move them otherwise.

paragraphs.heading: The Bouma cycle
paragraphs.text: Bouma gave the first proper description of turbidites in 1962. Studying deepwater sediments, he recognised intervals within fine-grained deep-water shales that started at pebble conglomerates and ended in shales, getting finer upward. This was odd, since it had been assumed that tractional flow had no way to carry coarse sediment into the abyssal depths. A Bouma cycle starts at an erosional contact with a coarse bed of pebble to granule conglomerate, grades up through sandstones, and ends in laminar siltstone and shale. The succession represents currents going from strong to waning. A complete cycle is unusual to see, because later turbidity currents may erode the unconsolidated upper parts.

paragraphs.heading: Denser currents
paragraphs.text: Bouma's progression is now recognised as applying to turbidites laid down by low-density turbidity currents. As the sand concentration of a flow rises, collisions between grains create dispersive pressures that hinder further settling of grains. Turbidites from high-density turbidity currents therefore develop a slightly different set of structures. This set is known as the Lowe sequence, and it complements the Bouma sequence without replacing it.

paragraphs.heading: Not only in the deep sea
paragraphs.text: Density-based flow is not confined to the deep ocean, though turbidites are particularly well represented there. Lahars on the sides of volcanoes, mudslides and pyroclastic flows all create it. Pyroclastic flows especially can produce sequences strikingly similar to turbidites.

paragraphs.heading: What turbidites record and hold
paragraphs.text: Turbidites from lakes and fjords can give dated evidence of how often landslides happened, along with the earthquakes presumed to have formed them. The dating uses radiocarbon or varves above and below the turbidite. Turbidite sequences are also classic hosts for lode gold deposits. At Bendigo and Ballarat in Victoria, Australia, miners have taken out more than 2,600 tons of gold from deposits in a thick succession of turbidites. Given time, turbidite deposits that have built up and lithified may become reservoirs of hydrocarbons.
